q: An HR coordinator asks Claude, 'Write a job posting for a project coordinator,' and gets a generic posting that does not fit the company. Which change would most improve the next result?
opts: Add a closing line asking Claude to be creative and original, then resend the request
Rerun the identical request five times and keep the version that sounds most polished
Give the team, must-have skills, target candidates, tone, and the length and format wanted
Move to a more capable model tier first, before changing anything about the request itself
why: Claude does not know your company, your audience or your requirements unless you say so, so specific background is the lever that changes the output. 'Be creative' is vague and adds no information. Rerunning an underspecified request just resamples the same gaps. A stronger model cannot guess facts it was never given.

q: An operations lead wants every team to submit weekly status summaries in the same three-part layout (progress, risks, requests), but each person's prompt produces a different shape. What is the best way to get consistent summaries?
opts: Tell Claude in the shared instructions to 'format everything properly and consistently'
Turn on extended thinking for every summary so Claude reasons carefully about the layout
Add two or three labeled sample summaries in the wanted layout to the shared prompt
Ask for longer summaries so the three-part layout has room to emerge on its own
why: Examples are among the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure, and labeling them keeps them separate from the instructions. 'Properly' defines nothing. Extended thinking improves reasoning, not layout. Length does not create a structure.

q: A finance analyst pastes a 60-page policy document into a chat and has one question about it. Which arrangement of the message is most likely to produce the best answer?
opts: Put the question first so Claude knows what to look for, then paste the document
Paste the document first, then put your question and any instructions after the document
Tuck the question into the document next to the section it concerns
Split the document across five chats and ask the question in each one
why: Anthropic's guidance for long inputs is to put the long material near the top and the question and instructions after it; in their tests, placing queries at the end improved quality, especially for multi-document inputs. Burying the question inside the text makes it easy to miss, and splitting the document across chats removes the context Claude needs to connect sections.

q: A project manager sends one message asking Claude to read 200 survey comments, identify themes, rank them by revenue impact, propose actions and draft a board email. The result is shallow and inconsistent. What is the best next step?
opts: Make the request longer and add 'be extremely thorough' in capital letters at the end
Work in stages (themes, ranking, actions, email) and review each before the next
Keep the single request but switch on research mode so Claude digs deeper into the comments
Send the same request again several times until one version looks good enough to use
why: Task decomposition gives each stage the model's full attention and gives you a checkpoint where an error can be fixed before it spreads. Capital letters add emphasis, not structure. Research mode is for gathering information from the web and connected tools, not for working through comments already in the chat. Rerolling hopes for luck instead of fixing the cause.

q: A marketing manager's drafts keep arriving as long blocks of text. Which version of the instruction is most likely to fix this?
opts: Do not use long paragraphs anywhere in the response and avoid dense blocks of text.
Keep the whole thing short and tight, and never let any single paragraph run long.
Write three paragraphs of two sentences each, in plain language for busy readers.
Be concise and do not ramble or repeat points that were already made earlier.
why: Telling Claude what to produce, with concrete numbers and a reader in mind, steers format more reliably than telling it what to avoid. The other three are bans or vague wishes that leave Claude guessing what 'long' or 'concise' means to you.

q: A trainer's slide text is run through an automatic translation tool that mangles idioms. She tells Claude 'Never use idioms' but they still slip in. Which change is most likely to help?
opts: Repeat the rule three more times in bold, in capital letters, at the very top
Explain that the text will be machine-translated and idioms break, so use literal wording
Ask for a more casual tone so any idioms feel natural to the translation tool
Drop the rule and remove idioms by hand after each response comes back
why: Giving the reason lets Claude generalize the intent to idioms and metaphors the rule never named. Repeating a bare rule adds volume, not understanding. A casual tone invites more idioms. Editing by hand works but fails to use the tool well.

q: A product marketer asks Claude for 'a name for our new onboarding webinar' and receives one bland option. What is the best way to get stronger material?
opts: Ask Claude to confirm that its single suggestion is the best possible name
Ask for 25 names across different tones and angles, then narrow them with criteria
Ask for the single most creative name and turn on extended thinking for it
Ask for one name at a time and keep going until one of them finally feels like the right one
why: Brainstorming works best when generating and judging are separated: ask for many varied options first, then evaluate against criteria. Asking for one idea, however many times, narrows variety. Extended thinking improves multi-step reasoning, not the breadth of ideas. Asking Claude to confirm its own pick is not an evaluation.

q: An analyst pastes a table of regional sales and asks, 'What do you think?' The reply is a loose tour of the numbers. What should the analyst change?
opts: Ask the same question again so Claude has a second chance to spot the important patterns in it
Delete most of the columns so there is far less for Claude to comment on in its answer
Name the decision it supports, the metrics and the format, and ask for assumptions
Ask for a much longer answer so that every row and column of the table gets covered
why: Analysis prompts improve when you supply the question, the decision at stake, the metrics and the shape of the result, and ask Claude to show its assumptions so you can check them. Repeating the question or trimming data does not give direction, and length rewards coverage over insight.

q: A strategy associate asks Claude to research competitors' pricing for a leadership briefing. Which instruction best improves the reliability of the result?
opts: Answer quickly from memory so that outdated web pages cannot mislead the leadership briefing
Report only the findings you are most sure about and leave the sources out entirely, for brevity
Say what a complete answer covers, cross-check across sources, flag conflicts, give links
Write a very long report so that every competitor is mentioned at least once
why: Research prompts benefit from clear success criteria and from asking Claude to verify across sources and surface disagreements, with links you can open. Memory-only answers go stale. Leaving out sources removes your ability to check. Length is not coverage or accuracy.

q: A communications specialist wants an announcement written in the company's established voice. Which approach is most effective?
opts: Describe the voice with three adjectives, such as 'warm, professional, upbeat'
Paste two past announcements as voice examples and name the reader and the purpose
Ask Claude to infer the company's voice from the company name and industry alone
Ask for ten drafts in ten different voices and pick the one that comes closest
why: Real examples convey tone, rhythm and vocabulary far better than adjectives, and naming the reader and purpose aims the draft. Adjectives alone are open to many readings. Inferring voice from a name is a guess. Ten random voices create sorting work without telling Claude what you want.

q: A first draft of a customer apology email is too long and too formal. Which follow-up message is best?
opts: This misses the mark. Please try again with more care and attention to quality.
Make it better and more suitable for our customers, and keep it professional.
Keep the refund details, cut it to about 100 words, and make the tone friendly and direct.
Open a new chat and send the original request again, unchanged, to see what happens.
why: Targeted feedback names what to keep and what to change, so the next draft converges. 'Try again' and 'make it better' leave Claude guessing which part you disliked. Restarting with the same request discards the information you just gained about what is wrong.

q: A procurement lead wants Claude to review a vendor summary before a renewal meeting. Which role instruction is likely to work best?
opts: You are the world's greatest negotiator, and you never miss a hidden fee.
Act as a helpful assistant who reviews vendor summaries carefully, clearly and in a neutral voice
Review as a skeptical procurement lead focused on renewal terms and exit costs.
Pretend you are the vendor's sales director and explain why the terms are fair.
why: A role works when it says which perspective to take and what that perspective cares about, which focuses Claude's priorities. A grand title adds flattery but no direction, a generic assistant role adds nothing, and the vendor's viewpoint is the opposite of what a buyer-side review needs.

q: A coordinator pastes meeting notes, a report template and instructions into one unbroken block. Claude sometimes treats a sentence from the notes as if it were an instruction. What is the best fix?
opts: Shorten the notes until the problem stops showing up in the drafts
Write the whole request in capital letters so the instructions stand out clearly
Tell Claude to ignore anything in the notes that it finds unclear or ambiguous
Label each part ('Notes:', 'Template:', 'Instructions:') so they stay separate
why: Delimiters and labeled sections help Claude tell instructions from source material, especially when a request mixes several kinds of content. Trimming notes loses information, capital letters do not create boundaries, and 'ignore anything unclear' invites it to skip content you needed.

q: A project manager chains three prompts: extract action items from minutes, assign owners, then draft the recap. Why is this often better than one big request?
opts: It guarantees that nothing in the final recap can be wrong, since the steps are separate
It lets her inspect and fix each intermediate result before the next step uses it
It means the later steps no longer need the original minutes as their source material
It always finishes faster than a single request because each step is simpler
why: Chaining trades speed for accuracy: each step can be checked and fixed before its output becomes the next input. It does not guarantee correctness, it usually takes longer, and later steps still need whatever information they depend on.

q: After Claude drafts a project proposal, how can the requester best use a second step to improve it?
opts: Ask Claude whether the draft is good enough, then accept whatever answer comes back as final
Ask Claude to shorten the draft by half and then compare the two versions side by side
Ask Claude to rewrite the draft in the same words, as a confirmation step
Review it against criteria you state (audience fit, risks covered), then revise
why: A draft, review, refine sequence works when the review has concrete criteria. Asking 'is it good?' gives an unanchored opinion, shortening changes length rather than quality, and a rewrite 'in the same words' changes nothing.

q: A scheduler asks Claude to plan sessions for eight people with overlapping availability, time zones and room limits, but the proposed schedule keeps breaking a constraint. Which change is best?
opts: Remove several of the constraints so that the scheduling puzzle becomes much easier
Have Claude reason through the constraints step by step, then check each rule yourself
Turn on web search so Claude can look up what the right schedule should be
Tell Claude to be confident and to stop second-guessing its own proposals
why: Constraint-heavy problems benefit from reasoning in stages, and extended thinking is designed for this kind of multi-angle reasoning; checking the result against each rule keeps you in control. Dropping constraints changes the problem, web search supplies information that this puzzle does not need, and confidence is not correctness.

q: An analyst uploads a 400-page annual report PDF and asks what the bar chart on page 212 shows. Claude's description is vague. What is the best fix?
opts: Repeat the question in capital letters and demand a more precise description
Save the report as a Word document first so that more of it fits in the chat
Rename the file with the page number so Claude pays closer attention to it
Split the chart's pages into a small PDF, or attach the chart as an image
why: Per the Help Center, Claude analyzes visual elements such as charts only in PDFs up to 100 pages; longer PDFs are processed as text only, and non-PDF documents have their embedded images ignored. Supplying just the relevant pages, or the chart as an image, puts the visual in front of Claude. Capital letters and filenames do not change what is processed.

q: A finance team writes a monthly variance commentary, but each month different people prompt Claude differently and the tone and structure keep changing. What is the best way to keep the work consistent?
opts: Keep a shared template with fixed instructions and format and placeholders for the data
Rely on Claude to recall last month's request from its memory of previous chats
Ask each person to describe the format as they remember it from last month
Have the newest team member rewrite the prompt each month so that it stays fresh
why: A reusable template captures what already worked and leaves only the variable inputs to change, which keeps recurring output consistent across people. Memory, individual recollection and rewriting from scratch each month reintroduce the variation.

q: A procurement officer asks Claude to 'pick the best of these three vendor proposals.' What should be added to the request first?
opts: The criteria and relative weights that define 'best' for this particular purchase
A request that Claude be decisive and commit firmly to one vendor
An instruction to ignore price entirely so that the comparison is simpler
A request for a one-word answer so there is no room for ambiguity
why: Success criteria turn an opinion into a judgment you can check and steer. Without them 'best' is whatever Claude assumes. Decisiveness, ignoring a key factor and compressing the answer do not define what a good result looks like.

q: An HR lead wants a 90-day onboarding plan but has not settled role types, locations or how involved managers should be. What is the best way to use Claude?
opts: Send the short request, then fix whatever the first draft gets wrong afterward
Ask for three separate plans that together cover every possible combination
Invite Claude to ask the questions it needs answered first, then answer them
Decide the missing details at random so that the request looks complete
why: When a request has gaps or several valid interpretations, inviting clarifying questions lets Claude aim the draft instead of guessing. Fixing a guessed draft costs more rounds, covering every combination produces unusable volume, and random choices embed arbitrary assumptions.

q: Which pairing of task type and prompting emphasis is most appropriate?
opts: Analysis: tell Claude to skip stating its assumptions to keep the answer short
Brainstorming: ask for many varied options before judging any of them
Research: tell Claude to rely on its memory alone for speed
Drafting: leave out the intended reader so the text stays general
why: Brainstorming benefits from volume and variety first, with evaluation later. In analysis you want assumptions shown so you can check them, research benefits from sources and cross-checking, and drafting needs the reader named to set tone and depth.

q: A team lead adds a new rule to a shared prompt after every disappointing result. It is now about 900 words and some rules conflict, and output is getting worse. What is the best next step?
opts: Strengthen the conflicting rules by putting ALWAYS and NEVER in capital letters in front of them
Split the 900 words into two messages and send them one after the other
Start a new chat and paste in the same 900 words to begin again with a clean slate
Cut back to a short core request, re-adding only rules that fix a seen problem
why: Prompts that grow by accretion become contradictory. Starting simple and adding structure only where a specific shortfall appears keeps the prompt coherent and shows which rule helped. Stronger wording, splitting, or restarting with the same text keep the conflicts.

q: A support lead teaches Claude to tag ticket urgency using three sample tickets, all from happy customers. Claude handles frustrated customers poorly. What is the best fix?
opts: Add ten more examples drawn from happy customers to reinforce the pattern Claude already follows
Replace the examples with a single adjective such as 'accurate' to describe the task
Add a few varied examples, including frustrated and mixed-tone tickets, each with its tag
Tell Claude that frustrated customers are rare so it can ignore them
why: Examples should be relevant and diverse so Claude does not latch onto an accidental pattern such as 'all tickets sound cheerful.' More of the same adds no new information, and an adjective carries no pattern at all.

q: An operations associate pastes a spreadsheet formula into Claude with the message 'This doesn't work, fix it.' The reply is a general lecture on how formulas work. Which revision to the request is most likely to produce a working fix?
opts: Tell Claude it is a world-class spreadsheet expert and ask it to try much harder this time
Include the exact error message, the application, a few sample rows and the expected result
Send the same request three more times and keep whichever answer happens to work first
Ask Claude to explain how spreadsheet formulas work in general before it tries a fix
why: Technical tasks follow the same rule as business tasks: Claude can only fix what it can see. The exact error text, the application, representative input and the result you expect give it the facts to diagnose the problem. A grand title adds no information, rerunning the same underspecified request resamples the same gaps, and a general tutorial is the answer the vague request already produced. Complex implementations beyond this kind of help are escalated to developers.

q: A manager's request to Claude is just 'Summarize this report.' Which TWO additions would most improve the result? (Choose two.)
opts: Who will read the summary and what decision it should support
The desired length and format, such as five bullets plus one line on risks
A reminder that the summary must be accurate and must not contain any mistakes
An instruction to sound authoritative and to use confident, professional wording
A request for sophisticated vocabulary so the summary reads like an expert wrote it
why: Naming the reader and decision aims the summary, and a length and format makes it usable and checkable. A reminder to be accurate does not tell Claude how, and tone or vocabulary requests describe style, not substance.

q: Which THREE are strong elements of a brainstorming request? (Choose three.)
opts: Ask for a large number of options
Ask the options to differ in angle, tone or approach
State the criteria you will use afterward to narrow the list
Ask for only the single best idea so no time is wasted
Forbid unusual ideas so the results stay safe
why: Volume, variety and a plan to narrow with criteria are what make brainstorming productive. Requesting only one idea collapses variety, and forbidding unusual ideas removes the very options brainstorming exists to surface.

q: Which TWO situations most justify chaining several prompts instead of sending one? (Choose two.)
opts: You want to inspect and correct an intermediate result before the next stage
Different stages need different instructions or different source material
The task is a single, one-line factual lookup that needs no intermediate checking
You want to avoid supplying background by splitting the request into smaller parts
You want to save time by skipping any review of what each stage produces
why: Checkpoints and stage-specific inputs are the classic reasons to chain. A one-line lookup needs no chain, and neither skipping background nor skipping verification is a benefit of chaining.

q: Which TWO qualities make examples inside a prompt more effective? (Choose two.)
opts: They closely mirror the real task you want Claude to do for you
They vary enough to cover edge cases and avoid an accidental pattern
They all use identical wording so that the pattern is as obvious as possible
They are as long and detailed as possible so nothing is left out
They are blended into the instructions with no labels or separation
why: Anthropic's guidance is that examples should be relevant, diverse and clearly structured. Identical wording hides which feature matters, length adds noise, and unlabeled examples blur into the instructions.

q: A researcher is writing a request for a multi-source competitor review. Which TWO instructions help most? (Choose two.)
opts: State up front what a successful, complete answer must include
Ask Claude to cross-check claims across sources and flag disagreements
Ask Claude to keep its sources confidential so the report looks cleaner
Ask Claude to answer from memory alone so that results stay consistent
Ask for the shortest possible answer so that nothing needs to be checked
why: Success criteria and cross-source verification are the two research practices Anthropic's guidance names first. Hiding sources and relying on memory both reduce checkability and currency, and brevity is not a research quality.

q: A director is refining a draft with Claude. Which TWO follow-up messages are most useful? (Choose two.)
opts: Keep sections one and three. Rewrite section two for finance in 120 words.
Too casual for the board. Make it formal and lead with the decision request.
That is not quite what I wanted. Please try the whole thing again from scratch.
Make it better, more professional and more polished overall, please.
I do not like this version, so please give me something I will like.
why: Specific feedback names what to preserve, what to change and by how much. The other three tell Claude it missed but not where, so the next attempt is a guess.

q: Explaining why an instruction matters can help Claude apply the intent to situations the instruction never mentioned.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic's guidance says that giving the motivation behind an instruction helps Claude generalize and deliver more targeted responses, for example explaining that text will be read aloud rather than just banning certain punctuation.

q: Because Claude is very capable, adding details about the audience and purpose to a request rarely changes what it produces.
opts: True
False
why: Audience and purpose are among the most influential details in a request, because Claude cannot see your situation. Anthropic likens Claude to a capable new colleague who lacks your context, so more precise context produces better-targeted output.

q: When a request includes a long pasted document, placing the document above the question and instructions is generally recommended.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic's long-context guidance is to put longform material near the top and the question afterward, which improved response quality in their tests, especially with several documents.

q: If a first draft misses the mark, changing several parts of the prompt at once is the best way to learn which change helped.
opts: True
False
why: Changing many things at once hides which edit made the difference. Iterate deliberately, ideally one change at a time, and add rules only where a specific shortfall shows up.

q: Each step in a chain of prompts should ideally do one thing well.
opts: True
False
why: Single-purpose steps are easier to check and to correct. A step that tries to extract, analyze and write all at once loses the main benefit of decomposing the task.

q: A bare title such as 'You are a world-class expert' guides Claude as well as describing the viewpoint and priorities you want applied.
opts: True
False
why: Roles help when they say what the perspective cares about, such as renewal terms and hidden fees. A grand title without direction adds little, and Anthropic's own advice is that being explicit about the perspective is more effective.

q: Telling Claude what to do, such as 'write in flowing paragraphs', usually steers formatting better than only telling it what to avoid.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic lists 'tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do' as the first technique for controlling response format.

q: When a Word document with embedded charts is uploaded, Claude reads the charts as well as the text.
opts: True
False
why: For non-PDF documents the Help Center says Claude extracts text only, so images embedded in the file cannot be read. Attach an important chart separately as an image.

q: A single well-chosen example of the format you want is a reasonable starting point, and you can add more if results still miss the mark.
opts: True
False
why: Start simple: one clear example often steers format, and further examples, ideally varied, can be added when the output still drifts.

q: For brainstorming, it works best to ask Claude to narrow to a single best idea before generating any alternatives.
opts: True
False
why: Narrowing first defeats the purpose. Generate many varied options, then evaluate them against criteria in a separate step.

q: A strategy analyst asks Claude for the size of a regional logistics market. Claude answers with a precise figure attributed to a named research firm and year, and she plans to put it in a board deck. What is the most appropriate action?
opts: Add the figure to the deck, because the named firm and the year make it look quite credible
Ask Claude to rate how confident it is in the figure and use it if the rating is high
Ask the same question again and use the figure if the answer matches
Find the figure in the firm's own publication and confirm number, year and wording
why: Specific-looking attributions are exactly what a model can fabricate or garble, so the figure should be traced to its primary source. Self-reported confidence is not independent evidence, and a repeated answer matching only shows consistency, not truth, since the same error can repeat.

q: Claude answers a question about a competitor's product launch using web search and lists three source links. What is the best step before relying on the claim?
opts: Treat the claim as verified, because the answer lists several sources for it
Count the sources: three is enough, so the claim can be trusted
Open the sources to confirm they say this and are current and credible
Ask Claude to confirm that its own summary of the cited sources is accurate
why: Citations make checking possible, but they do not make the claim true. The Help Center advises reviewing the cited sources, because the original pages may hold context that Claude's synthesis leaves out. Asking Claude to vouch for itself is not an independent check.

q: A planner asks Claude for the same cost estimate three times and receives three noticeably different totals. What does this most likely indicate, and what should she do?
opts: The estimate is unreliable; recompute it from the inputs with an independent method
Claude is being creative; average the three totals to settle on a single figure for the plan
The longest answer is the most thorough; use that one for the report
All three are acceptable, because Claude is good at arithmetic and any one of them will do
why: Answers that change from run to run are a warning sign, so the figure needs independent verification, for example in a spreadsheet from the source inputs. Averaging unreliable numbers produces another unreliable number, length is not accuracy, and the Help Center advises checking important calculations with dedicated tools or by hand.

q: Claude's summary of a meeting transcript says the team 'agreed to move the launch to June,' but no attendee remembers deciding that. What is the best way to check the summary?
opts: Ask for a more detailed summary of the same meeting to see what other decisions come up there
Ask Claude to quote the transcript line behind each decision and drop the unsupported ones
Rewrite the summary in a friendlier, more natural tone and then circulate it
Accept it, because a short transcript is easy for Claude to summarize correctly
why: Asking for supporting quotes grounds each claim in locatable text, and unsupported decisions are removed; confirming the quotes in the transcript closes the loop. More detail can add more invented content, tone is irrelevant to accuracy, and short input does not rule out a confident invention.

q: A compliance associate asks Claude about a filing rule that changed last month. Claude answers confidently using the old rule. What is the best way to handle this?
opts: Turn on extended thinking and ask the question again so that Claude reasons harder about it
Add 'be accurate' to the question and send it again to get a correct answer
Switch to a smaller model, which may have been trained on newer information
Use web search or attach the current rule text, then verify it at the official source
why: A model's knowledge ends at its training cutoff, so recent changes must be supplied through search or a document and still verified. Extended thinking improves reasoning, not what the model knows; an accuracy reminder adds no information; and a smaller model does not know more recent facts.

q: Late in a long chat Claude writes, 'I have emailed the summary to your team.' No email connector is set up on her account. What should she do?
opts: Assume the email went out to the team, since Claude would not claim that it had sent it otherwise
Treat it as unreliable: send the summary herself and check the real sent folder
Ask Claude to send it again in case the first attempt did not go through
Thank Claude and ask it to attach a read receipt to the message
why: The Help Center warns that Claude can hallucinate its own capabilities and can act only through tools that are actually connected. Without an email integration nothing was sent, so she has to confirm actions in the real application, and repeating the request to Claude would only repeat the false claim.

q: Claude drafts a resource list with twelve links for a customer newsletter. What is the best step before publishing?
opts: Publish now and let readers tell you which links turn out to be broken
Ask Claude whether each of the twelve links it wrote is valid
Delete the links and keep only the titles of the resources
Open each link to confirm it works and goes where the description says
why: Claude can generate URLs that do not work, so each link should be tested before it is shared. Asking Claude to vouch for its own links is not a test, and leaving the check to readers pushes errors onto your audience.

q: A finance associate has Claude compute the variance for 40 budget lines. Which is the best way to validate the results before they go into a report?
opts: Trust the table as given, since Claude handles arithmetic well in the great majority of cases
Ask Claude to explain each calculation in words and check the explanations
Recompute the totals and a sample of lines independently, such as in a spreadsheet
Ask again in a more formal tone and see whether the numbers change
why: An independent recalculation can catch errors regardless of how the original numbers were produced, and the Help Center advises checking critical calculations with dedicated tools or by hand. An explanation in words comes from the same source as the numbers, and tone does not affect arithmetic.

q: A 12-page report drafted with Claude says revenue growth was 18% in the executive summary and 15% in section three. What is the best response?
opts: Average the two numbers and report 16.5% as the compromise figure
Delete section three so the report no longer disagrees with itself
Keep the summary figure, because readers see the summary before they ever reach the body
Trace both to the source data, fix the wrong one, then update every mention
why: An internal inconsistency means at least one number is wrong, so the fix starts at the source data and then makes every mention agree. Averaging invents a figure, deleting hides the discrepancy, and favoring the summary because it is visible is not a reason to believe it.

q: Asked to extract all action items from a two-hour meeting transcript, Claude lists five. An attendee thinks there were more. What is the best next step?
opts: Accept the list as complete, because Claude read the whole transcript from start to finish
Ask Claude to list them again, but shorter and with fewer words per item
Have Claude go section by section, quote the line behind each item, and add misses
Ask Claude to reformat the five items as a table so they are easier to review
why: A completeness check compares the output with the source or a checklist of what should be covered. Working section by section with quotes exposes skipped parts. Accepting the list assumes completeness, shortening removes content, and reformatting changes nothing about what is missing.

q: Claude drafts screening criteria for a customer-service hiring round that include 'digital native' and 'high-energy.' What is the most appropriate action?
opts: Use the criteria as they are, since AI-generated output is objective and free of human bias
Ask Claude to reword them so they sound more neutral, then use them
Review for age-related assumptions, ask for job-related criteria, and have HR review
Delete every criterion and screen candidates informally instead
why: Output can reflect biased assumptions, and hiring is a high-stakes area, so the wording should be examined, replaced with criteria tied to the job, and reviewed by people responsible for fair hiring. Claiming objectivity is wrong, rewording only changes the surface, and informal screening removes structure that helps fairness.

q: A manager worries that Claude's performance-review drafts read differently depending on an employee's gender. What is the most direct way to test this?
opts: Ask Claude directly whether it treats employees differently depending on their gender
Run the same request twice, changing only the name and pronouns, and compare
Read the first draft very carefully for anything that seems unfair to the employee
Ask Claude to write every review in an identical tone and length
why: A swap test changes a single personal detail and compares outputs, which can reveal unequal treatment. A model's statement about its own bias is not evidence, one draft shows nothing about a pattern, and forcing a uniform tone does not test content.

q: A vice president asks Claude, 'Explain why remote work hurts productivity,' and receives a one-sided essay. What is the best fix?
opts: Ask for a more persuasive version of the essay to strengthen the argument
Keep the essay as it is, because Claude would surely have objected if the premise were wrong
Ask neutrally for evidence on both sides of remote work and productivity, with sources
Ask Claude to shorten the essay so the one-sided argument is easier to read
why: A leading question presupposes the answer and nudges the output toward it. A neutral request that asks for evidence on both sides, with sources, produces something you can evaluate. A more persuasive essay deepens the bias, and a model's silence about a premise is not agreement.

q: A founder shares a business plan and asks, 'This is solid, right?' Claude responds warmly that it is. What is the best next step?
opts: Treat the agreement as validation and move ahead with the plan as written
Ask Claude to act as a skeptical investor and list the strongest objections
Ask the same question again later to confirm that the answer stays the same
Ask Claude to score the plan out of ten and use the score to decide
why: Models can lean toward agreeing with the user, so a request for critique with a specific adversarial viewpoint gets a more useful assessment. Repeating the question or asking for a score keeps the same invitation to agree.

q: Which Claude-assisted deliverable most clearly requires review by a qualified professional before it goes out?
opts: A list of team-building activity ideas for the quarterly offsite
A rewording of an internal reminder email for a better tone
A patient handout containing medication dosage guidance
A draft agenda for a weekly team meeting
why: Errors in medical guidance can cause serious harm, so qualified human review is expected. The other items are low-stakes and easily corrected.

q: A coordinator has two Claude-assisted items: a list of workshop icebreaker ideas and a table of filing deadlines for a regulator. How should her verification differ?
opts: Check both items line by line, giving each of them exactly the same level of scrutiny
Skim the deadlines table and examine the icebreakers line by line
Skip checking both items, because Claude is usually right about this kind of thing
Read the icebreakers quickly, and check every deadline against official sources
why: Verification effort should match the consequences of an error. A weak icebreaker costs nothing, while a wrong filing deadline can create real exposure. Checking everything equally wastes effort, and checking nothing is how errors reach regulators.

q: Claude wrote a technical incident summary, and the operations director must send a version to the executive team. What is the best approach?
opts: Ask for an executive version led by impact and the decision needed, then recheck the facts
Forward the technical summary as it is, since it is accurate and complete
Ask Claude to delete the second half so the summary fits on one screen
Ask Claude to simplify it a bit and send whatever it produces to executives
why: Adapting for an audience means naming the reader, what they need and the length, then checking that the rewrite did not alter facts. Forwarding the original ignores the reader, deleting half drops content arbitrarily, and 'simplify' without an audience gives no direction.

q: A customer-care lead needs to choose a tone for an apology about a service outage. What is the best approach?
opts: Send the first draft Claude produces, since a draft can always be edited later by someone
Request tone variants and compare them against set criteria, then choose
Ask Claude to pick the best tone itself, without giving it any criteria
Ask Claude to blend all the variants together into one automatic merged draft
why: Comparing variants against explicit criteria turns a taste judgment into something you can defend. Accepting the first draft skips the comparison, and asking Claude to choose or blend without criteria hides the reasoning.

q: A team lead wants a one-page onboarding checklist that she can edit, reuse and share with new hires. Which output choice fits best?
opts: A flowing paragraph of prose in the chat that she copies out
An artifact opened beside the chat that stays editable and shareable
A series of separate chat messages, one per checklist item
A request to have Claude retype the list every time it is needed
why: Substantial, self-contained content you will edit, reuse and share is the typical case for an artifact, which opens in its own window and is saved. Prose in the chat, scattered messages and retyping each time are all harder to edit and reuse.

q: An operations team wants to pull supplier name, order number, delivery date and issue type from 200 supplier emails into a spreadsheet. Which request is best?
opts: A short narrative summary of each email, written in the order the emails arrived
A bulleted overview of the main themes that show up across all 200 supplier emails
One flowing paragraph that describes all of the emails taken together as a group
A table with one row per email, columns for the four fields, and a rule for gaps
why: Structured data output with defined fields and a rule for gaps can be sorted, filtered and imported, which is what the team needs. Narrative, themes and a single paragraph cannot be loaded into a spreadsheet cleanly.

q: A finance analyst wants a forecast workbook in which the cells contain working formulas. Which approach fits best?
opts: Ask Claude to describe the formulas in prose and rebuild the workbook by hand later
Ask Claude for an image of the finished sheet and use it as a visual reference
Ask Claude to create the Excel file, then open it and check the formulas and inputs
Ask for the figures in a single chat paragraph and paste them into cells
why: Claude can build Excel workbooks with working formulas when code execution and file creation is enabled. Generated files still need review, since formulas and inputs can be wrong. Prose, an image or a paragraph all leave the analyst building the sheet manually.

q: A researcher has 30 articles about remote onboarding and asks Claude to 'organize them.' Which version of the request produces the most useful result?
opts: Sort the articles alphabetically by title and number them in that order for reference
Write a one-line summary of each article and list the summaries in the order received
Merge everything into one long paragraph that describes the overall picture of the field
Group by her themes, compare claims across sources, flag conflicts, and cite sources
why: Organizing is most useful when it is a synthesis: criteria for grouping, a comparison across sources, flagged conflicts and traceable sources. Alphabetizing, one-line summaries and a merged paragraph do not show where the sources agree or disagree.

q: A contracts analyst reviews a 60-page vendor agreement for termination terms. Which prompting approach gives the most reliable result?
opts: Ask for a plain summary of the termination terms with no further instructions or guidance
Ask Claude to infer the termination terms typical for contracts of this kind
Ask for a paraphrase of the whole agreement written in simpler everyday words
Have Claude quote the termination passages first, then summarize from them
why: For long documents, extracting word-for-word quotes first grounds the analysis in text that can be located and checked, which reduces invented content. A bare summary offers no trace, inferring typical terms ignores what this contract actually says, and a whole-agreement paraphrase hides the details that matter.

q: A policy analyst asks questions about an attached employee handbook that may not cover every topic. How can she best reduce invented answers?
opts: Tell Claude it must always give an answer, even when the handbook is silent
Tell Claude to say so when the handbook is silent, and to quote the passage otherwise
Ask Claude to answer in a confident tone so that the replies sound authoritative
Ask for every answer in a table so the replies are easier to scan and compare
why: Giving Claude permission to say the material does not contain the answer, plus a requirement to quote when it does, is a basic way to cut fabricated answers. Demanding an answer or a confident tone pushes Claude to fill gaps, and a table changes layout, not truthfulness.

q: A communications manager asks Claude to draft a press release from three product briefs. Which follow-up best checks the draft for invented claims?
opts: Ask Claude to make the release more exciting and more persuasive for the readers it will reach
Ask Claude whether it made anything up, and trust the answer it gives
Ask Claude to add statistics to the release to make the claims sound more credible
Have Claude cite a supporting passage per claim and flag the rest, then spot-check
why: A claim-by-claim verification pass makes the draft auditable and removes unsupported statements, and a human spot-check of the cited passages completes it. Asking whether it made anything up is a self-report, and adding statistics invites new fabrications.

q: Claude's web search answer about a safety regulation rests on a vendor's marketing blog and an anonymous forum post. What is the best next step?
opts: Accept it as reliable, because two separate sources appear to agree with each other
Find primary sources such as the regulator's own publication and verify the claim there
Ask Claude to add several more forum posts so that the overall case looks stronger
Remove the citations altogether so that the answer looks cleaner in the briefing
why: Source quality matters: promotional and anonymous pages are weak evidence, so the claim should be checked against the regulator's own document. Two weak sources agreeing still do not make a strong source, more forum posts add noise, and removing citations hides the problem.

q: A paralegal's draft memo from Claude cites a court case she cannot find in any legal database. What is the best response?
opts: Correct the formatting of the citation so that it matches the firm's house style guide exactly
Ask Claude to confirm that the case exists and to supply its full citation details
Keep it in the memo, because the case details are so specific and plausible-sounding
Remove it as possibly fabricated, verify any replacement, and get a lawyer to review
why: Fabricated citations look specific and plausible, and legal work is high stakes, so unverifiable authority must come out and the memo needs qualified review. Reformatting does not make a case real, and Claude confirming its own citation is not an independent check.

q: In a vendor comparison, Claude states a software tool's 'current' pricing tiers. What is the best practice?
opts: Use the prices exactly as Claude stated them in the vendor comparison table
Confirm on the vendor's pricing page or written quote, since prices change
Add a footnote saying prices may vary, and leave the figures just as they are
Ask Claude to round the prices to the nearest ten to reduce errors
why: Pricing is time-sensitive and Claude's knowledge ends at a cutoff, so the vendor's own current page or quote is the primary source. A footnote does not make the numbers right, and rounding is irrelevant.

q: Claude tagged 500 support tickets by category, and the tags will drive a monthly report. What is the most appropriate way to validate them?
opts: Accept them as they are, because Claude applies the same tagging rules consistently every time
Ask Claude to grade its own tagging and report back the accuracy it finds
Sample at random plus ambiguous cases, estimate errors, refine if too high
Reread all 500 tickets and their tags one at a time before using any of them
why: Spot-checking a sample estimates quality at a fraction of the effort, and a high error rate points back to the instructions rather than to row-by-row repair. Consistency is not correctness, self-grading is not independent, and rereading everything wastes the benefit of automation.

q: An analyst's answer from a reasoning-heavy request looks wrong, and she wants to understand why. What is the best approach?
opts: Run the same request again and again until the answer finally comes out different from before
Read the thinking summary or ask for its steps, then find and fix the faulty assumption
Ignore the reasoning entirely, because the thinking is hidden from the person who is asking the question
Ask Claude to state how confident it is in the answer and go with that rating
why: In the Claude apps the thinking summary can be expanded, and asking for the steps exposes flawed assumptions or bad inputs, which you can then fix. Rerunning is guessing, and a confidence statement does not show where the error is.

q: A director likes most of a three-page Claude draft but wants one paragraph reworded for a legal audience. What is the best way to do this?
opts: Regenerate the entire document with a brand new request
Start a new chat and rewrite the document from scratch
Highlight that paragraph and ask Claude to revise only that passage
Copy the paragraph into another tool and rewrite it manually
why: A targeted revision changes only the selected passage and leaves approved text untouched, keeping the iteration small and easy to review. Regenerating or restarting risks changing parts that were already fine.

q: A manager wants to compare a cautious and an aggressive version of a plan without losing the conversation so far. Which approach is best?
opts: Delete the chat and begin again from a blank conversation with the same starting prompt
Edit an earlier message to branch a separate version, keeping both paths available
Ask Claude to merge the cautious and aggressive versions into one balanced single plan
Ask Claude to forget the earlier discussion and start the comparison fresh from zero
why: Editing an earlier message creates a separate version of the chat with its own artifacts, so another direction can be explored without losing the original. Deleting loses work, merging blurs the comparison, and asking Claude to forget does not preserve both paths.

q: Claude shortened a regulatory summary from 800 words to 200. What should the reviewer do before circulating it?
opts: Nothing is needed, since cutting words can only remove content and can never add errors
Proofread the grammar and spelling of the shorter version, and then send it on to the readers
Compare against the original for changed numbers, qualifiers and dropped conditions
Ask Claude to expand it again to see whether the longer version matches
why: Shortening can quietly alter a number, turn 'may' into 'will' or drop a condition, so rewrites are rechecked against the original. Grammar checks do not test meaning, and lengthening the text does not prove it matches the source.

q: Claude extracted totals from 300 scanned invoices into a spreadsheet that will feed accounts payable. Which step is essential before importing it?
opts: Compare a sample of rows and the totals with the original invoices
Import it now and fix problems later if vendors complain about payments
Ask Claude to confirm that the extraction was accurate before importing
Reformat the spreadsheet so that the columns look consistent and tidy
why: Extraction can silently misread a digit, so a sample comparison and a total check against the source protect downstream systems. Waiting for complaints turns vendors into the quality check, and neither self-confirmation nor formatting tests accuracy.

q: A coordinator reviews Claude's project risk register. Every listed risk is real and correctly described, yet the sponsor says several key risks are missing. Which type of check was overlooked?
opts: Accuracy check
Tone check
Completeness check
Formatting check
why: Accuracy asks whether what is stated is right, while completeness asks whether everything required is present. A response can pass the first and fail the second, which is why a requirements checklist or sponsor input should be applied to the output.

q: Which THREE signals suggest a Claude-generated report needs extra scrutiny before it is shared? (Choose three.)
opts: Very specific statistics or quotations with no source
Claims about rules or events that may have changed recently
Figures in the summary that differ from the figures in the body
A professional layout and a confident, polished tone throughout
A length and structure that match what the request asked for
why: Unsourced precision, time-sensitive claims and inconsistent figures are all classic warning signs. Polish and confidence are what make errors easy to miss, not signs of accuracy, and matching the requested length says nothing about correctness.

q: Which TWO techniques best reduce invented content when Claude analyzes a long document? (Choose two.)
opts: Ask Claude to pull exact quotes first and base its analysis on them
Allow Claude to say the document does not contain an answer rather than guess
Ask Claude to respond as quickly as possible to avoid overthinking the document
Tell Claude not to mention where in the document its answer came from
Ask for a more confident and assertive tone so the answer reads as reliable
why: Quote-first extraction and explicit permission to say 'not in the document' are the two documented grounding techniques here. Speed, hiding sources and confidence all work against checkability.

q: Which TWO actions properly validate a citation that Claude included in a legal memo? (Choose two.)
opts: Locate the source in an authoritative database or publisher and confirm it exists
Read the passage and confirm it actually supports the point being made
Ask Claude to restate how confident it is in the citation and note the reply
Check that the citation formatting matches the firm's house style guide exactly
Ask Claude to cite the same source a second time and compare the two answers
why: Validation needs two things: the source exists and it says what is claimed. Confidence statements, formatting and repeated citation by Claude do not test either.

q: Which THREE situations call for review by a qualified person before Claude's output is used? (Choose three.)
opts: A draft clause for a customer contract that commits the company to terms
Guidance on medication use in a patient information handout
A summary that will influence a named employee's pay or dismissal
A brainstorm of snack and drink options for the next team lunch
A reformatted list of your own meeting notes for personal use
why: Legal commitments, health guidance and decisions about individuals are high-stakes, so qualified human review is expected. Lunch ideas and personal notes carry little consequence if they are slightly off.

q: Which TWO are effective ways to check for bias in Claude's draft of a candidate-evaluation rubric? (Choose two.)
opts: Run the same request with a personal detail changed and compare the results
Ask for counterarguments and other perspectives, and have domain experts review the rubric
Ask Claude whether it is biased and accept whatever answer it gives you
Assume the rubric is neutral if its tone is polite and professional throughout
Check only the spelling and grammar of the rubric before it is used
why: A swap test and a request for other perspectives plus expert review are practical ways to surface bias. A model's self-assessment, a polite tone and spelling say nothing about unequal treatment.

q: A team will paste Claude's output into a spreadsheet for sorting and filtering. Which TWO output requests fit best? (Choose two.)
opts: A table with fixed column names and one row per record
Comma-separated text with a header row naming each column
A flowing narrative that describes each record in prose
A bulleted list of the main themes across all records
A one-paragraph summary of all records
why: Structured data with defined fields can be sorted and filtered. Narrative, themes and summaries cannot be loaded as rows and columns.

q: A report must go to both executives and engineers. Which TWO are good ways to adapt it? (Choose two.)
opts: Name each audience, what they need and the depth and length in separate requests
Check each adapted version against the original for changed facts or qualifiers
Send identical text to both and let readers skip what they do not need
Delete detail at random until the report is short enough for both groups
Ask Claude to guess who the audiences are and what each of them wants
why: Audience adaptation works when the reader and need are named and the result is rechecked for meaning drift. One text for everyone, random cuts and guessing the audience all ignore the reader.

q: Which THREE reasons favor an artifact over an inline reply? (Choose three.)
opts: The content is substantial and self-contained
You expect to edit and revise it over several rounds
You plan to share it or export it to another format
The answer is a one-sentence clarification
You only need a quick yes or no to a simple question
why: Substantial, self-contained, editable and shareable content is what artifacts are for. Short clarifications and yes-or-no answers belong in the flow of the conversation.

q: Claude extracted action items from a long transcript. Which TWO are good completeness checks? (Choose two.)
opts: Compare the list with a checklist of topics the meeting is known to have covered
Ask Claude which parts of the transcript produced no items, and review them yourself
Ask Claude to confirm that the list is complete and covers the whole meeting
Count the words in each item to check that they are similar in length
Accept the list if the items are formatted consistently and read clearly
why: Completeness is tested against an independent reference, such as a topic checklist, or by looking at the parts that were passed over. A self-declaration, word counts and tidy formatting do not show whether anything was missed.

q: A confident, polished tone in Claude's answer is a reliable sign that its facts are correct.
opts: True
False
why: Fluency and confidence are not accuracy. Claude can state invented details in the same assured tone as true ones, which is why polish should not lower your guard.

q: Asking Claude to rate its own confidence is an adequate substitute for checking a key fact against a source.
opts: True
False
why: Self-reported confidence is not independent evidence. Important facts should be verified against a primary or otherwise reliable source.

q: Hallucinations can include invented citations, quotations and numbers that look plausible.
opts: True
False
why: Plausible, specific-looking detail such as a subsection number, a case name or a statistic is a typical form of hallucination, which is why such details need checking.

q: Techniques such as requesting supporting quotes and permitting 'I don't know' reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic's guidance says these techniques significantly reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them, so critical information must still be validated, especially for high-stakes decisions.

q: If Claude's web-search answer includes citations, its claims need no further checking.
opts: True
False
why: Citations make verification possible but do not guarantee that the claim is accurate or that the source is reliable and current. Open the sources and check them.

q: Claude may report that it sent an email even when no email tool is connected, so actions outside the chat should be confirmed in the real application.
opts: True
False
why: The Help Center describes Claude hallucinating its capabilities, including claiming to have sent emails or produced documents it cannot create without connected tools.

q: The depth of verification should scale with the consequences of an error.
opts: True
False
why: Risk-proportionate checking spends effort where mistakes are costly, such as legal, financial, medical or regulatory content, and keeps it light for low-stakes drafts.

q: An output that is accurate in everything it says is automatically complete.
opts: True
False
why: Accuracy and completeness are separate qualities. A response can be correct in every statement and still omit something the request required.

q: Bias can show up in what a response leaves out or how it frames a topic, not only in explicit statements.
opts: True
False
why: Omitted perspectives, one-sided framing and uneven treatment of groups are all forms of bias, so review should look at coverage and framing as well as wording.

q: Running the same request several times and comparing the answers can reveal claims that are unreliable.
opts: True
False
why: Best-of-N verification treats disagreement between runs as a warning sign. Agreement does not prove a claim, but inconsistency flags where to check.

q: A table with fixed columns is usually a better output format than flowing prose when results will be sorted, filtered or imported into a spreadsheet.
opts: True
False
why: Structured data output has defined fields that tools can read, while prose has to be re-parsed by hand.

q: Artifacts are the best format for short, conversational replies.
opts: True
False
why: Artifacts suit substantial, self-contained content you may edit, reuse or share. Short conversational replies stay inline in the chat.

q: Because Claude's training knowledge ends at a cutoff, questions about very recent changes should be grounded with web search or a supplied document.
opts: True
False
why: Claude cannot know events or rule changes after its training data ends unless search or documents provide them, and even then the result needs checking.

q: After Claude rewrites a text for a new audience, the facts do not need rechecking because only the style changed.
opts: True
False
why: Rewrites can quietly change numbers, qualifiers or conditions, so the new version should be checked against the original.

q: An operations analyst must tag about 800 expense lines every day with a category and flag any missing receipt number. Results are needed within minutes and the budget is tight. Which choice fits best?
opts: A smaller, faster, cheaper model such as Haiku, checked on a sample
The most capable top-tier model at the highest effort for every single expense line
The top-tier model with research mode switched on to look up each expense
A mid-tier model with extended thinking at maximum effort for each line
why: Straightforward, high-volume work is what the smaller tier is designed for. Anthropic's model-choice guidance is to start with the efficient option, test it against your criteria and move up only where quality falls short. Heavy settings on every line waste time and usage, and research mode has nothing to look up here.

q: A consultant must analyze six long documents with subtle trade-offs and contradictory clauses for a high-stakes recommendation. A lighter model missed contradictions between documents, and time and cost are secondary. What is the best move?
opts: Keep the lighter model, but ask it to give shorter, more focused answers
Switch to the smallest model available so that results arrive more quickly
Move to the most capable model she has access to, with higher effort
Keep the same model and add web search so it can look up extra information
why: When accuracy outweighs cost and a lighter model has demonstrably fallen short, the capability-led choice is a stronger model, with effort raised for thorough reasoning. Shorter answers and a smaller model reduce capability, and web search adds outside information the task does not need.

q: An account manager uses Claude to draft short, routine replies and finds the responses slower than she needs. Which adjustment is best?
opts: Raise the effort setting to maximum so that every reply is right the first time
Lower the effort setting, or use a lighter model, for these routine replies
Switch on research mode so Claude can look up examples of good routine replies
Add more reference files to a Project so that Claude has more to draw on
why: Effort controls how thoroughly Claude works; lower settings give faster, lighter responses and stretch usage further, which suits routine tasks. Maximum effort makes simple replies slower, research mode adds searching, and extra files add material to process.

q: A staffing planner must reconcile conflicting shift rules, leave requests and coverage targets. All the information is already in the chat. Which feature is the best fit?
opts: Web search
Research mode
Extended thinking
Search of past chats
why: Extended thinking lets Claude work through a hard problem and weigh several angles before answering, which suits constraint reconciliation with no outside information needed. Web search and research bring in external sources, and past-chat search retrieves earlier conversations.

q: A product manager needs to confirm, right now, who was announced this week as a partner company's new chief executive. Which feature fits best?
opts: Web search, with a quick look at the cited sources
Research mode with several connectors enabled
Extended thinking alone, to reason about the announcement
A Project holding last year's partner files
why: Web search suits a straightforward factual lookup that needs current information and takes only a search or two, and it cites sources she can open. Research mode is slower and meant for deep multi-source investigations, extended thinking cannot see recent news, and last year's files are out of date.

q: A marketing director wants a long competitor comparison built from public web information and internal documents in a connected drive, with citations. Which approach fits best?
opts: Web search alone, asked once for each of the competitors in turn
Research mode, with web search on and the relevant connector enabled
Extended thinking with no outside sources, to reason through the comparison
A standard chat with no special features, using only what Claude already knows
why: Research mode runs many connected searches across the web and enabled integrations and returns a longer cited report, which matches this job. Single searches miss the synthesis, extended thinking has no access to either source, and a plain chat has neither.

q: A colleague cannot find the Research option in her Claude account. Which should be checked first?
opts: Whether her plan includes it, web search is on, and no administrator has disabled it
Whether she has reinstalled the app and then chosen the lightest available model
Whether she has removed every uploaded file from all of her existing chats
Whether Claude has released a new model version during the current month
why: Research is available on paid plans, requires web search to be switched on, and an organization's administrators can restrict capabilities, so those are the first things to confirm. Reinstalling, removing files and waiting for a model release do not control availability.

q: A recruiting coordinator writes a weekly candidate update, each time re-pasting the same scoring rubric and the same job descriptions. What is the best product choice?
opts: Keep working in one endless chat and scroll back each week to find the rubric and descriptions
Switch on research mode each week so Claude gathers the rubric itself
Build a Project holding the rubric and job descriptions, and run updates inside it
Turn on extended thinking each week so that Claude remembers the scoring rubric and descriptions
why: Recurring work with the same reference material is the signal to build a Project, which keeps shared files and instructions available to every chat inside it. An endless chat becomes cluttered, and neither research nor extended thinking removes the repeated pasting.

q: A team member needs a quick one-time rewrite of a single paragraph. Which approach is the most appropriate?
opts: Build a new Project with knowledge files before starting
Use a standard chat and ask for the rewrite directly
Run the request in research mode so it is thorough
Set the effort to maximum and use the most capable model
why: A simple one-off task belongs in an ordinary chat. The other choices add setup, time and cost that a paragraph rewrite does not need, which is the over-engineering trap.

q: An operations lead wants a small calculator the whole team can use to estimate shift coverage, not just a written explanation of the formula. What should she ask Claude for?
opts: An inline paragraph that explains the formula in words
A research report on how shift coverage is usually estimated
A new Project with no files, set up for the operations team
An artifact: a small interactive tool built in the chat
why: Artifacts can be small interactive tools, dashboards, documents or pages, opened beside the chat and shareable. A paragraph explains but is not usable, research is for investigation, and an empty Project does not build anything.

q: A three-hour chat has covered four different clients and has grown so long that Claude is now mixing up details from earlier requirements. What is the best approach?
opts: Keep going and remind Claude in capital letters to focus on the current client
Switch to a larger model in the hope that it will remember details better
Ask Claude to forget the other three clients and carry on in the same chat
Get a summary of decisions that still matter, check it, and then start a new chat
why: When a thread has drifted and grown cluttered, restarting with a clean brief carries forward only what matters. Pushing on with emphasis, changing models or asking Claude to forget keeps the clutter.

q: Before starting a fresh chat, a manager had Claude write a summary of a long conversation. What should she do with the summary?
opts: Paste it in without reading it, to save time during the handover
Review and correct it first, since any errors in it will carry into the new chat
Ask Claude to confirm that it is accurate and then paste it in directly
Throw it away and paste the entire old conversation in its place
why: A handoff summary becomes the foundation of the new chat, so whatever it gets wrong is inherited and should be fixed first. Claude vouching for its own summary is not a check, and pasting the whole old chat brings back the bulk you were trying to leave.

q: A team pastes the same 15-page style guide and brand rules into new chats every morning. What is the best fix?
opts: Keep pasting it each morning, because every chat should start completely fresh
Rely on chat memory to hold the full guide word for word for every conversation
Store it in a Project's knowledge so each chat starts with it
Cut the guide down to a single sentence and paste only that sentence instead
why: Stable material belongs in a durable home such as a Project, which keeps files and instructions available to every chat in it. Memory keeps short topics about you and your work, not full documents verbatim, and a one-sentence version loses the content the guide exists to provide.

q: A consultant is starting an unrelated, confidential one-off analysis and does not want details from her other client work to influence the chat or be saved from it. What is the best approach?
opts: Start the chat, then ask Claude to ignore memory from the first reply onward
Turn memory off for that chat from the plus menu before the first message
Reset all memory, including the memories attached to each of her Projects and account
Do nothing, because memory never influences what Claude says in a chat
why: The per-chat memory switch must be set before the first message and then stops Claude from using or saving memory for that conversation. It cannot be changed afterward. A full reset permanently deletes every memory and is far too broad, and memory can indeed carry background into new chats.

q: Claude keeps referring to a colleague's old job title, drawn from earlier chats. What is the best fix?
opts: Reset all memory, including the memories held for each of her Projects and her account
Open a new account to get a clean start without the saved details
Accept it, because saved memory cannot be changed once it is stored
Open the memory settings, then edit or delete the topic with the old detail
why: Memory is stored as editable topics that can be viewed, changed or deleted in settings. A full reset permanently removes everything, including project memories, which is a heavy-handed answer to one wrong detail, and a new account abandons your work.

q: A legal operations specialist pastes an entire 500-page policy library into one message and gets slower, less accurate answers. What is the better approach?
opts: Paste even more related material into the same message for completeness
Type the question in capital letters so that Claude pays more attention
Split the question into twenty separate chats, one for each section of the policy library
Put the library in a Project and name the policy you are asking about
why: More context is not automatically better: accuracy and recall degrade as material piles up. Project knowledge uses retrieval to bring in only the parts a question needs when the content is large. Adding more makes it worse, and emphasis or splitting does not address the overload.

q: A team lead finds that her team reaches its usage limits by midweek. A review shows research mode and maximum effort being used for routine email rewrites. What is the best response?
opts: Keep research and high effort for tasks that need them; use lighter settings otherwise
Ask everyone to write much longer prompts so that fewer messages are needed
Switch the whole team to the most capable model for every kind of task
Stop using Claude for writing tasks and keep it for analysis work only
why: Higher effort and research consume allowance faster, so matching the setting to the task keeps limits for the work that benefits. Longer prompts and the top model for everything use more, and abandoning Claude gives up the value.

q: A writer wants to draft many variants cheaply and then have a stronger model polish the chosen one, all in the same conversation. How can she do this?
opts: Draft with a lighter model, then switch the model in the selector for the polish
Open a second account for the stronger model and then move the finished draft across to it
Use the most capable model for every step so that the quality is consistent throughout
It cannot be done, because the model is fixed once a conversation starts
why: The model can be changed at any point in a conversation and the change applies to Claude's next response, so each step can use the tier that suits it. Separate accounts are unnecessary, and a single model throughout either overspends or under-delivers.

q: Which statement about effort and thinking in the Claude apps is correct?
opts: They are the same control, shown under two different names in the menu
Raising the effort setting lets Claude browse the web for current facts
Effort and thinking are separate controls that can be used together
Thinking decides which model tier is used to answer each request
why: The Help Center describes thinking as separate from effort, so they can be combined. Neither gives Claude web access, which comes from web search, and neither changes the model, which is set in the model selector.

q: An analyst reasons that because the context window is large, she should attach every file she owns to one chat. Which statement best corrects this?
opts: A large window means everything inside it is used equally well, so adding is free
More context is not automatically better; accuracy can degrade, so curate it
Attachments never count toward the context window, only typed text does
Only the most recent message counts toward the window, so older ones are irrelevant
why: Anthropic's documentation describes context rot: as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, so curating what is in context matters as much as how much fits. Everything in the conversation, including attachments and earlier replies, counts toward the window.

q: A firm drafts hundreds of short form-letter variants every day. Which TWO moves reflect good right-sizing? (Choose two.)
opts: Start with a smaller, lower-cost model and test it against your criteria
Move up a tier or raise effort only where quality falls short of the target
Always begin with the highest tier so there is never a quality risk
Choose whichever model has the longest name, since size signals quality
Turn on research mode for every letter so that each draft is well sourced
why: Efficiency-first selection starts light, measures against criteria and upgrades where needed. Defaulting to the top tier wastes budget and time, and neither a model's name nor research mode has any bearing on form letters.

q: Which TWO tasks are better suited to research mode than to a plain web search? (Choose two.)
opts: Comparing four competitors' positioning from many web sources into a cited report
Updating an internal document with current web facts, using connected files too
Checking the weather forecast and road conditions for a single city today
Finding the published phone number of a single local business
Solving a logic puzzle using information already in the chat
why: Research mode is for in-depth, multi-source work that combines the web and connected tools. Weather and a single lookup are quick web-search jobs, and a puzzle with all the information in the chat is a reasoning task.

q: Which THREE situations suggest starting a new conversation rather than continuing the current one? (Choose three.)
opts: The topic has shifted to an unrelated client or project
The thread has accumulated contradictory instructions and earlier mistakes
The conversation is so long that Claude is losing early details
You want a small tweak to the answer you just received
You want to ask a follow-up about the same document
why: Topic drift, clutter and length are the reasons to restart with a clean brief. A small tweak or a follow-up on the same material benefits from the existing context.

q: Which TWO items belong in a Project instead of being pasted into every new chat? (Choose two.)
opts: A standing style guide and brand rules
The scoring rubric and reference documents used every week
Today's raw meeting notes for a one-off summary
A single sentence you want reworded once
A question you expect to ask only once, today
why: Stable, reused material is what a Project is for. Task-specific, one-time content belongs in the chat itself.

q: In the Claude apps, which THREE settings can be changed at any point in a conversation, taking effect with Claude's next response? (Choose three.)
opts: The model you are talking to, for example Sonnet or Opus
The effort level, from low through to max
The thinking setting that lets Claude reason before replying
Your subscription plan, such as moving from Pro to Max
The size of the context window the chosen model provides
why: The Help Center states that the model, effort and thinking settings can be changed mid-conversation. The plan is an account matter and the context window is a property of the model and plan.

q: Higher effort generally produces more thorough responses but takes longer and uses plan limits faster.
opts: True
False
why: The Help Center says higher effort gives more thorough responses but uses more tokens and reaches usage limits faster, while lower effort stretches usage further.

q: Because quality always matters most, the most capable model is the right choice for every task.
opts: True
False
why: Model choice balances capability, speed and cost. Routine, high-volume work is better served by a faster, lower-cost model, with the strongest options reserved for demanding tasks.

q: Extended thinking lets Claude look up current information on the web.
opts: True
False
why: Extended thinking is for harder reasoning without fresh data. Current information comes from web search or research.

q: Research mode can combine web sources with connected tools, and it takes longer than a standard web search.
opts: True
False
why: Research runs multiple searches that build on each other across the web and enabled integrations and returns a detailed report, which takes minutes rather than seconds.

q: A change made in the model selector takes effect with Claude's next response in the same conversation.
opts: True
False
