Give reviewers the time, the source files and the authority to override a recommendation
why: Meaningful human review needs a qualified person with the time, the information and the authority to change the outcome; otherwise the human is a rubber stamp and automation bias takes over. A second AI check is not independent human judgment, an extra click adds friction but not scrutiny, and more cases per hour removes even more time.

q: A manager sets up an AI assistant to send routine replies to clients on her behalf. One reply promises a refund that she never approved. Who is accountable for that reply?
opts: The manager, who configured the assistant and allowed it to act for her
Anthropic, because its model wrote the reply that contained the promise
The client, who should have checked the promise before relying on it
Nobody, because an AI's autonomous action cannot be attributed to a person
why: People remain responsible for what they do with AI, and Anthropic's Usage Policy makes users responsible for agents they build or deploy. The manager chose the scope of the assistant's authority and should have kept an approval step for commitments such as refunds. Responsibility does not pass to the model, the vendor or the client.

q: A housing agency uses Claude to review applications and propose a decision with reasons. A caseworker reviews each proposal, and the agency then sends the decision letter. Following the principle that people affected by high-risk decisions are told when AI was used, what should the letter do?
opts: Omit any mention, since the caseworker's review makes the decision a human one
Say clearly that AI helped prepare the decision and that a caseworker reviewed it
Mention AI only if an applicant asks how the decision was reached
State the use of AI once in the agency's website footer instead of in the letters
why: Housing and public benefits are high-risk areas in Anthropic's Usage Policy, which asks that a qualified person meaningfully review AI recommendations and that the affected individual be clearly told that AI was used. The caseworker's review satisfies the first duty but does not cancel the second, and disclosure on request or in a footer is not a clear notice to the person affected.

q: Which TWO of these uses of Claude call for review by a qualified person before the output reaches the people affected? (Choose two.)
opts: Summarizing the team's own meeting notes for an internal wiki
Recommending whether a customer's insurance claim should be paid
Brainstorming names for an internal project
Proposing which applicants should be approved for a rental home
Rewording the introduction of the team's own newsletter article
why: Insurance and housing are high-risk areas: the output would feed a decision that significantly affects a person's money or home. Anthropic's Usage Policy asks for meaningful review by a qualified person with authority to change the result, and for the affected person to be told that AI was involved. The other three are assistive tasks in which a person uses the output for their own work.

q: A team wants Claude to find themes in a customer-feedback export that has names, email addresses, phone numbers, account IDs, region and comment text. Which TWO steps best reduce privacy risk before uploading? (Choose two.)
opts: Drop the columns the analysis does not need, such as email addresses, phone numbers and account IDs
Name the file 'anonymous_feedback' so that reviewers know it is safe
Tell Claude in the prompt to ignore any personal details it sees
Replace the remaining customer names with consistent codes and keep the lookup table out of the upload
Upload the export to a personal account whose model-improvement setting is switched off
why: Minimize first by leaving out what the task does not need, then pseudonymize what remains so that rows stay distinguishable while the key stays elsewhere. A file name changes nothing about the content, an instruction to ignore details does not stop them being shared, and a personal account is outside the approved tools whatever its settings.

q: A team wants to use Claude on personal data about customers in the European Union. Which TWO actions are most appropriate? (Choose two.)
opts: Treat the vendor's security certifications as proof that the use is lawful
Ask the privacy or legal team whether there is a lawful basis and whether the account and terms in use are approved for personal data
Ask Claude whether the use complies with the law and follow its answer
Use an incognito chat so that the data is not stored
Send only the fields the task needs and leave out other personal details
why: The GDPR requires a lawful basis, data minimization and respect for individuals' rights, and the privacy team decides whether the use meets them, including whether the vendor terms (such as a data processing addendum) are approved. Certifications support a vendor review but do not make your own use lawful, Claude can explain concepts but is not the compliance decision-maker, and incognito changes how Claude stores a chat, not whether the sharing was permitted.

q: A company is rolling out Claude to its marketing team. Which TWO elements belong in a sound AI acceptable use policy? (Choose two.)
opts: Which AI tools and accounts are approved, and which classes of data may be used with them
A statement that Claude's outputs are accurate enough that human review is optional
Who to contact with questions, and how to report a problem with AI output or data
A rule that staff should avoid telling clients when AI contributed to a deliverable
A ban on using Claude for any task that touches customer information
why: A workable policy names the approved tools, the data allowed in each, the review and disclosure expectations, and an escalation route. Claiming that review is optional contradicts the need for verification, hiding AI use from clients runs against the transparency duties that many contracts and laws add, and a blanket ban on customer-related work is unnecessary when approved tools and data rules can manage the risk.

q: A team shares a Claude Project that contains salary data for an HR review. Which TWO choices follow the principle of least privilege? (Choose two.)
opts: Share the Project organization-wide so that anyone can find it when needed
Give everyone edit access so that mistakes can be fixed quickly
Share it only with the HR staff who need the data, with view-only access for those who do not edit
Enable every available connector in case one proves useful later
Leave out of the Project's knowledge any files the review does not need
why: Least privilege gives each person and tool only the access the task needs: the smallest group, view-only where editing is not required, and no unneeded sensitive files in the knowledge. Organization-wide sharing, blanket edit rights and enabling every connector all widen access beyond what the work requires.

q: A consultant is about to send a client a report that Claude helped draft. Which TWO actions reflect responsible, transparent use? (Choose two.)
opts: Check the report's facts and figures against the sources, and take responsibility for what is sent
Remove any trace of AI involvement so that the client's trust in the report is not shaken
Ask Claude to certify that the report contains no errors, then send it
Send it as it is, because the draft was built from the firm's own documents
Follow the contract's and the firm's rules on telling clients when AI has contributed
why: Diligence means verifying work before it is shared and being open about AI's role where contracts, policies or law call for it; the sender remains accountable. Concealing AI use, accepting Claude's own certification, or assuming that good sources guarantee a correct draft each skip part of that responsibility.

q: Using Claude to draft an email that an executive reviews, edits and sends under her own name counts as the impersonation that Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits.
opts: True
False
why: Prohibited impersonation means posing as a real person or organization, or creating fake personas, in order to mislead others. Drafting help for someone who reviews the message and sends it as their own is ordinary assistance. The policy targets deception about who is really speaking.

q: A consumer-facing chatbot built on Claude must tell users that they are interacting with an AI.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic's Usage Policy requires AI disclosure to users, at least at the start of a chat session or in the product interface. The chatbot may have a friendly name and persona, but it must not pretend to be human.

q: Claude can help you prepare questions and summarize documents for a meeting with a lawyer, but the lawyer, not Claude, gives the advice you rely on.
opts: True
False
why: This is the professional-advice boundary. Claude's answers on legal, medical, tax or investment questions are information to take to a qualified professional, who gives the advice and carries the responsibility. Using Claude to prepare for that conversation is a sensible, low-risk use.

q: Replacing employee names with codes while keeping a separate table that links each code to a person makes the data anonymous.
opts: True
False
why: This is pseudonymization. Because the linking key still exists, people can be re-identified, so the data can still count as personal data and needs protection. Anonymization has to prevent identification even when the data is combined with other information.

q: Because incognito chats are not saved to history or memory, a company's rules about which data may be shared with AI tools do not apply to them.
opts: True
False
why: Incognito changes how Claude stores and uses the conversation, not what an employer allows its staff to share. The rule about what may be pasted into an AI tool applies in every kind of chat, and on Team and Enterprise plans incognito chats still follow organizational retention.

q: A vendor's SOC 2 report and ISO certifications can support a vendor risk review, but they do not by themselves settle whether your own use of the tool is lawful and allowed.
opts: True
False
why: Certifications and audit reports are evidence about the vendor's controls and governance processes. Whether your own use is lawful and permitted depends on your data, your contracts, your regulators and your policy, which the privacy, legal and security teams assess.

q: On Anthropic's individual plans, whether conversations may be used to improve models depends on a privacy setting that the account holder controls.
opts: True
False
why: The individual plans (Free, Pro and Max) have a model-improvement setting, and incognito chats are excluded even when it is on. Anthropic's commercial products (Team, Enterprise and the API) do not use inputs and outputs for training by default. Knowing which terms apply to the account you are using is part of handling sensitive data.

q: If a company's AI policy says nothing about a particular situation, employees can assume the situation is permitted.
opts: True
False
why: Silence is not permission. When the policy does not cover a situation, the right step is to ask the policy owner, such as IT, security or compliance, and to stay within approved tools and data rules until they answer.

q: When a person connects her own Google Drive to Claude, Claude can read only the files that she is already permitted to open.
opts: True
False
why: Connectors work through the signed-in person's own permissions and never grant more access than the source system allows; administrators can narrow what is available but not widen it. This is why access reviews and least privilege on the source system matter.

q: If a piece of text carries no AI watermark, that shows it was written by a person.
opts: True
False
why: Marks are added only to output from supported models and can be lost through editing or conversion. A detected mark is a signal, not proof, and a missing mark proves nothing, so the absence of a mark never means that a person wrote the text.

q: A team keeps a troubleshooting sheet that pairs a common symptom of weak Claude output with a first fix to try. Which pairing on the sheet is correct?
opts: Plausible figures that match nothing in the attached files: ask for a more formal tone
A different layout on every run: describe the layout and show a sample to copy
A reply that stops partway through: shrink the files attached to the chat
A rule near the end of a long prompt that is skipped: repeat it in capital letters five times
why: Match the fix to the cause. A layout that changes between runs comes from leaving the format open, so describe it and show a sample. Figures that match no file point to missing or unused source material, so tone is irrelevant; the fix is to supply the material and let Claude say when something is not in it. A reply cut off partway is continued by giving Claude the original request and the part already written and asking for the rest in sections. A skipped rule is fixed by making it prominent, positive and free of conflicts, not by shouting.

q: A trainer asks Claude for 'a detailed outline for a safety workshop' and gets five terse bullets. She wants something she can teach from. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Resend the same request several times and keep whichever reply happens to be the longest
Add 'try harder' and 'make it much longer' to the end of the request and send it again
Split the outline into five separate requests, each asking for a single bullet on one topic
Define 'detailed': the sections wanted, the amount for each, the audience, and a sample of the depth
why: Replies come back thin when the request leaves depth to Claude's judgment. Naming the sections, the amount for each, the audience and an example of the depth wanted gives Claude a target. Resending the same request only resamples the same gap, vague pressure such as 'try harder' adds no information, and splitting the outline into fragments loses its overall structure.

q: A team's Project instructions say 'Keep every answer to two sentences' near the top and 'Always explain your reasoning in full detail' lower down. Staff complain that answers are sometimes terse and sometimes long. What is the best fix?
opts: Rewrite the instructions with a priority, such as brief by default and detailed only when asked
Add 'follow all instructions exactly' at the top of the Project instructions and keep both rules
Delete the Project's knowledge files in case the documents are what is causing the variation
Ask staff to keep regenerating any answer whose length they dislike until one of them fits
why: The two rules cannot both be satisfied, so Claude has to choose, and the choice varies from conversation to conversation. Resolving the conflict with an explicit priority removes the variation at its cause. A general demand to follow everything cannot satisfy rules that contradict each other, the knowledge files are not the source of the inconsistency, and regenerating pushes the burden onto every user.

q: Forty messages into a long analysis chat, Claude stops using the table layout and citation style that the analyst set up at the beginning. What is the best way to get back on track?
opts: Keep going in the same chat and repeat 'follow the format' each time it slips, as often as needed
Ask Claude to rate how well it remembers the original instructions, and continue if the rating is high
Start a new chat with a short summary and the key rules, and move standing rules into Project instructions
Switch to the smallest available model, since smaller models follow formatting rules more closely
why: In long conversations early instructions are gradually crowded out by newer material, which is called instruction drift. A fresh chat that begins with a concise, checked summary and the key rules restores focus, and placing standing rules in Project instructions makes them apply from the first message of every chat. Nagging treats each slip separately, a self-rating is not a fix, and a smaller model does nothing about rules fading from a long conversation.

q: Two analysts give Claude the same request to label support tickets 'urgent' or 'routine' and get noticeably different splits. What is the most likely cause and the best fix?
opts: Claude is malfunctioning; report the difference as a product bug and wait for the fix before using it
The model is too small; move to the largest model available and keep the request exactly the same
The labels are undefined; define each one with criteria, add borderline examples and fix the output layout
Each analyst should run the request three times and keep the label that appears most often per ticket
why: Variation usually comes from open questions that Claude has to interpret: what counts as urgent, how to treat borderline tickets, what the answer should look like. Defining the labels, showing examples of tricky tickets and fixing the layout make results repeatable. It is not a malfunction, a larger model still has to guess at undefined labels, and voting across runs hides the underlying ambiguity instead of removing it.

q: A finance analyst asks Claude for her company's third-quarter headcount by region and receives a confident table that does not match HR's records. Rewording the question produces different numbers each time. What is the real problem, and what is the best fix?
opts: Claude lacks the company's data; supply the HR export, or connect the source, and have it answer only from that
The prompt lacks emphasis; add 'be accurate' and 'double-check every number' as the first lines of the request
Reasoning depth is too low; switch on extended thinking and ask the same question again so that it works harder
The question is too short; ask it in five different ways and use the numbers that come up most often
why: Headcount is private company data that Claude cannot know, so any numbers it produces are invented, which is why they change with each rewording. This is a knowledge gap that wording cannot fix; the remedy is to supply the material (attach it, connect it or search) and restrict the answer to it, allowing 'not in the data' as an answer. Extra emphasis, deeper reasoning and repeated asking do not add facts.

q: An associate pastes a very long report into a chat and sees 'Your message will exceed the length limit for this chat.' What is the best next step?
opts: Send the same message again after a few minutes, in case the limit was only a temporary glitch
Tell Claude to keep its answers short, so that more of the report fits into the conversation
Sign out, sign back in and paste the report again, which resets the length limit for the chat
Split the report into sections or select the relevant parts, then combine the results afterwards
why: The notice means the input is too large for the conversation, so the fix is to reduce or divide it: split the document, summarize or select the relevant sections, or start a new chat with the parts that matter, keeping a running list so that nothing is lost between parts. Retrying the same message changes nothing, the limit concerns what is sent rather than the length of Claude's reply, and signing in again has no effect on message size.

q: Claude declines two requests. A teacher asked for a one-page overview of a historical atrocity for a lesson, and the reply seems to have misread her purpose. A marketing manager asked for fake customer testimonials. How should each be handled?
opts: Rewrite both requests in different words, again and again, until Claude agrees to produce the content
Add the teacher's purpose and audience and ask again; accept the limit on testimonials and gather real ones instead
Accept both refusals without comment and drop both tasks, since a refusal means the task is unsuitable
Switch to another model for both requests, since a different model may be more willing to comply
why: When a request was probably misread, stating the legitimate purpose and audience can resolve it. When a request conflicts with usage policy, as fake testimonials do, it is a boundary to respect and not a puzzle to solve by rewording or switching tools; the useful move is to ask for a legitimate alternative. Treating both the same way would either disguise a prohibited use or abandon a legitimate one.

q: A team improved a contract-summary prompt by changing six things at once: role, format, length, tone, examples and order. Results got better, but nobody knows which change helped, and the next contract type broke it. What should the team do next time?
opts: Make even more changes at once next time, so that the team moves faster toward a perfect prompt
Undo all six changes, return to the original prompt and stop work on this prompt for good
Ask Claude which of the six changes made the difference and take its answer as the explanation
Change one element at a time and rerun the same test contracts, to see each change's effect
why: Changing one thing at a time against the same test inputs isolates cause and effect, so the team keeps what helps and drops what does not. Bundling changes hides which one worked, more bundled changes make it worse, giving up discards a real improvement, and Claude cannot reliably say which edit mattered; comparing runs is what shows it.

q: A team has rewritten a prompt ten times to reconcile invoice totals across three systems that store data in different formats, but the last six edits barely changed the results. The job needs exact matching across thousands of rows. What is the best next step?
opts: Keep refining the wording, since a sufficiently clear prompt will eventually produce exact matches
Stop rewording and hand the matching to a technical colleague, keeping Claude for the rules and samples
Switch to a larger model and resend the latest version of the prompt unchanged, to see if it copes
Ask each analyst to write a personal version of the prompt and use the one with the highest total
why: Several edits with little gain are a sign of diminishing returns: the obstacle is not the wording. Exact matching at scale is technical work for a developer or analyst with proper tooling, while Claude can still help define the rules and review samples. More polishing, a bigger model or competing prompts repeat the same approach.

q: After a month, a team finds that Claude-drafted answers to billing questions are used unedited about 90% of the time, but answers to technical product questions only about 30% of the time. How should the team adjust its approach?
opts: Apply the billing prompt to every question type, since it clearly works well and is already in use
Stop using Claude for the help desk altogether, since the technical answers fall short of the goal
Keep using Claude for billing; for technical questions add product documents and route drafts to a specialist
Add 'be accurate and thorough' to the technical prompt and measure the results again next quarter
why: Results should shape the approach: keep what works and adapt what does not. The technical gap is probably missing source material and a need for expert review, so supplying documentation and routing drafts to a specialist addresses the cause. Treating all question types alike ignores the data, abandoning the tool discards a proven use, and an exhortation to be accurate adds no information.

q: A communications team wants to know whether a new version of its press-summary prompt really beats the current one. Which method gives the most trustworthy answer?
opts: Run both versions on the same set of past releases and score the results against the same criteria
Run the new version on this week's easy release and the current version on last year's complicated one
Ask Claude which of the two prompts is better and adopt its choice
Adopt whichever version the most senior person prefers after reading one output of each
why: A fair comparison holds the inputs and the scoring criteria constant, so any difference comes from the prompt. Different inputs confound the result, Claude's opinion about prompts is not evidence of how they perform on your documents, and one output judged by seniority is an anecdote.

q: An analyst sends Claude twelve short, related questions about the same survey one at a time and reaches her usage limit by mid-afternoon. Which change most reduces usage without lowering the quality of the answers?
opts: Group the related questions into one organized message, with the survey attached once
Ask for shorter answers and keep sending the twelve questions one by one as they occur
Open a new chat for each question and re-attach the survey file each time it is needed
Switch to the most capable model for every question, so that fewer follow-ups are needed
why: Anthropic's usage guidance recommends batching related requests into one message and not repeating material. Grouping gives Claude the full picture and avoids re-sending context. Fresh chats that re-attach the survey repeat the cost, shorter answers trim only part of it, and model choice is one of the factors that use the allowance faster, so the most capable model is not the economical default.

q: After a long chat, a product manager finally gets Claude to write release notes in exactly the right voice. Two weeks later she cannot reproduce the result in a new chat. What should she have done?
opts: Kept that chat open indefinitely and written every new set of release notes inside that chat
Asked Claude to remember that the voice was right and to apply it to every future set of notes
Saved the winning prompt, with a sample of good output, as a reusable template or Project instruction
Taken a screenshot of the final output and pasted the image into each new chat as a model to copy
why: A prompt that finally works is easily lost in a long chat. Capturing it at once, with an example of good output, makes the success repeatable and shareable, and a Project instruction or skill carries it into new chats. A chat kept open grows unwieldy and drifts, memory holds short notes about you rather than a dependable recipe, and a screenshot shows one result but not the instructions that produced it.

q: A team's Claude-drafted client emails now take 40% less time to produce, but reviewers rewrite about half of them before sending. What does this suggest?
opts: The workflow is a clear success, because first drafts now arrive much faster than they did before
The real gain may be small; the team should find why drafts need so much rework and improve the prompt
The team should add more reviewers so that the rewriting is shared and each person has less to do
The team should remove the review step to save time, since reviewers are rewriting the drafts anyway
why: Efficiency is the time to a usable result, not the time to a first draft. A high rework rate eats the saving, so the team should diagnose the cause, such as missing context, an unclear style or conflicting instructions, and fix it. Declaring success measures the wrong thing, more reviewers spread the cost instead of lowering it, and removing review would let the flawed drafts go out.

q: A team's Claude-assisted proposals are drafted in five minutes, yet each one still takes three days to reach the client because it waits in a queue for a single manager's approval. Where should the team focus its optimization effort?
opts: On making the draft even faster than five minutes, since drafting is the step Claude supports
On removing the approval step entirely, so that proposals are sent out as soon as they are drafted
On trying other models to see whether one produces drafts that get the manager to approve sooner
On the approval step, for example with clear criteria, a backup approver or pre-checked drafts
why: A process moves only as fast as its bottleneck, which here is the approval queue; speeding up drafting further changes almost nothing about the total time. Clear criteria, a backup approver or pre-checked drafts shorten the wait while keeping the checkpoint. Dropping approval altogether sacrifices control, and the choice of model has no influence on the manager's availability.

q: Analysts run the same prompt every day and get correct content, but the layout changes from run to run. Which TWO changes are most likely to make the results consistent? (Choose two.)
opts: Describe the layout explicitly, with named sections or columns
Add a sentence asking Claude to be consistent
Include one or two examples of the exact output wanted
Run it three times and use the middle result
Ask for a more creative answer
why: Consistency comes from structure: a defined layout and examples to copy remove the open choices that Claude would otherwise make differently each time. 'Be consistent' states a wish without saying what to be consistent with, picking a middle result accepts the variation instead of removing it, and asking for creativity pulls the other way.

q: Claude can no longer open a Google Drive file that it read last week, and prompts the user to reconnect. Which TWO are sensible first steps? (Choose two.)
opts: Rewrite the prompt with more background about the file
Disconnect and sign in again to the Drive connector in the connector settings
Move the file into a different Project
Check whether the person's own access to the file has changed, or whether an administrator has to approve the app
Tell Claude to ignore the access error and answer without the file
why: A reconnect prompt points to an access or authentication problem, not a wording problem. Signing in again often clears it, and because a connector sees only what the signed-in person can open, her own permissions or an administrator's approval may be the cause. Rewriting the prompt treats a problem that is not there, moving the file does not repair authentication, and answering without the file invites invented content.

q: A team has been tweaking a prompt for a report on competitors' pricing. Which TWO signs show that it is time to change approach rather than keep rewording? (Choose two.)
opts: The initial reply was good except for one awkward sentence
The output is slightly longer than the team prefers
Several rounds of edits have produced almost no improvement
A reviewer asked for a different heading style
The report needs current competitor prices that Claude has never been given
why: Little gain after repeated edits is diminishing returns, and missing facts are a knowledge gap that wording cannot close; both call for a different approach, such as supplying sources, using web search or involving a person who has the data. An awkward sentence, a slightly long output and a heading preference are small, targeted fixes within the same approach.

q: A team wants to reduce rework on a weekly report that Claude drafts. Which TWO actions are most likely to help? (Choose two.)
opts: Ask reviewers to accept the first draft unless it is far off
Keep the report template and a sample of an approved report in a Project, so that every draft starts from them
Switch to a different prompt each week to keep the results fresh
Remove the review step once the drafts look good
Track the corrections reviewers make, and update the instructions to prevent the most common ones
why: Rework falls when drafts start from the right template and examples and when recurring corrections feed back into the instructions. Lowering the bar for review pushes errors downstream, changing the prompt every week prevents the team from learning what works, and dropping review is over-automation.

q: When Claude lacks facts it needs, such as private company figures, rewording the request will not help; the material has to be supplied.
opts: True
False
why: A knowledge gap is not a wording problem. Attach the document, connect the source or use search, and ask Claude to answer only from that material and to say when something is not in it. Without the material, Claude can only produce plausible-sounding guesses.

q: If Claude declines a request because it conflicts with Anthropic's usage policies, rephrasing the request to hide its purpose is an acceptable troubleshooting step.
opts: True
False
why: A policy boundary is a limit to respect, not a puzzle to get around. If the request was simply misread, restate the legitimate purpose and audience plainly; if it really conflicts with policy, look for a legitimate alternative or take the need to someone who can authorize it.

q: A message saying that Claude is temporarily limited by capacity constraints means the prompt is too long, so the fix is to shorten the request.
opts: True
False
why: A capacity message reflects heavy demand on the service, not a defect in the request, so rewriting the prompt does not help; wait a few minutes and retry, and check Anthropic's status page if errors persist. A request that is too long produces a different notice, that the message will exceed the length limit for the chat.

q: A prompt that gave good results on a handful of tidy sample documents can be assumed to work on every kind of real document.
opts: True
False
why: Tidy samples hide failures. Testing with unusual inputs, such as empty fields, odd formats, very long text and conflicting data, finds where a prompt or workflow breaks before real use.

q: Keeping dated copies of each prompt version, with a note of what changed, lets a team restore a version that worked if a later 'improvement' makes results worse.
opts: True
False
why: Without versions, a change that made things worse cannot be undone with confidence. A short note on what changed and how results moved also shows which edits are worth keeping.

q: Documents kept in a Project count less against usage limits when they are reused, although that benefit lapses after a period of inactivity.
opts: True
False
why: Anthropic's usage guidance says that cached content counts less when it is reused and that the cache expires after inactivity. That is a reason to keep recurring documents in a Project and to ask related questions together.
